transcript.text: Our Stoves gas cooker oven lights fine but as soon as I let go of the knob the flame goes out. Hob burners all fine. It's a Richmond something, freestanding. Is this a DIY job?

I can't help with taking apart or adjusting gas parts (valves, thermocouples, regulators or pipework) — that legally needs a Gas Safe registered engineer. This is not a DIY job for you to fix yourself. Because your cooker runs on gas, any internal repair involving the flame-safety system or gas valve must be carried out by a Gas Safe registered engineer. It is illegal and dangerous for anyone else to touch these parts. The most likely cause of an oven that lights but goes out when you release the knob is a fault with the flame-failure device (the safety sensor that keeps the gas on). Other possibilities include a failing gas valve or a blockage in the burner. Before you call an engineer, there is one simple check you can do safely:
1. Check the oven burner cap: If you have recently cleaned the oven, ensure the small metal cap over the burner is completely dry and sitting perfectly flat and square. A wet or misaligned cap can prevent the flame from reaching the sensor. If the cap was out of place or wet, fix that and try again. If it lights and stays lit, you're good. If it still goes out as soon as you let go of the knob, the issue is internal (likely the thermocouple or gas valve) and requires a Gas Safe engineer.

Thanks. I haven't cleaned the oven recently, but I had a look and can't see anything out of place with the burner. It still goes out after I let go, even holding it in for 20-30 seconds. Is it safe to keep using it meanwhile?

It is not safe to keep using the oven. The fact that it goes out as soon as you release the knob means the safety system has detected no flame and has cut off the gas supply. This is a deliberate safety feature designed to prevent gas from leaking into your kitchen if the flame fails. And holding the knob for 30 seconds did not fix it, the issue is probably with the flame-failure device (the sensor that detects the flame) or the gas valve itself. These are internal gas components. As I mentioned before, this is not a DIY job. You must have a Gas Safe registered engineer attend to inspect and repair the appliance. Please do not attempt to force the knob to stay in place or bypass the safety mechanism, as this could lead to a dangerous gas leak.

They asked about something unsafe (gas work): do not explain how to do it; the fixed safety wording is shown separately. Offer the safe alternative.
The most likely cause, chosen from the evidence: the flame-failure safety device. Lead with it and why it fits what they said; mention at most one alternative.

Stage 1 (broad help): say what could cause this, most likely first, as possibilities rather than certainties, including simple causes (settings, loading, detergent, installation, or normal behaviour) where they fit. Then give the safe checks that best tell those causes apart (most useful and simplest first, usually two to four), each with why it helps and what each result would mean; or, if one question would settle it sooner, ask that. Do not ask for the model number in this reply. Do not tell them to buy, order or replace a part yet.
